# Modeling cards and shuffled decks

We followed online code to produce
```{r do1}
suits <- c("Spades", "Hearts", "Diamonds", "Clubs")
ranks <- c("Ace", 2:10, "Jack", "Queen", "King")
# Combine ranks and suits to make 52 unique cards
deck <- paste(rep(ranks, 4), rep(suits, each = 13))
```
A deck is a vector with 52 elements.
This vector "models" a deck of playing cards.

With R's `sample` function, we can model shuffling.
We use `set.seed` to obtain a reproducible random
number generation state.

```{r lkshuf}
set.seed(1234)
sample(deck, 1)
sample(deck, 1)
set.seed(1234)
sample(deck, 1)
```

A reproducible series of draws of the "top card" from the repeatedly shuffled deck.
```{r lk1}
set.seed(123)
draws = replicate(1000, sample(deck,size=1))
mean(table(draws))-1000/52
hist(table(draws), 20)
plot(table(draws), las=2, cex.axis=.7)
```




# Exploring the US CDC API

We visited the CDC dataset section:

![CDC topics](./cdcsets.jpg)

I used the old-fashioned httr package to extract a file
on waterborne illness.
```{r lkcd,eval=FALSE}
library(httr)
z = GET("https://data.cdc.gov/api/v3/views/5xkq-dg7x/query.json")
zc = content(z)
```

To see the tree structure of the data
```{r lkli,eval=FALSE}
library(listviewer)
jsonedit(zc)
```


We will have exercises related to this dataset.  But let's have
one exploration.  Let's look for the largest waterborne outbreak
in the dataset.  How should we compute `nill` so
that the following succeeds?  Can you verify the report?
